To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the prevalence of depressive symptoms in late life increases with increasing age and 2) the prevalence of depression in late life is higher in women and in those who have lower levels of education and/or lower income, who have a history of depression and/or have a family member who has been diagnosed with depression.

1) The risk of developing late-life depressive symptoms is predicted by early-life depressive symptoms, early-life cognitive functioning and early-life physical functioning; and 2) The risk of late-life depressive symptoms increases as early-life depressive symptoms increase and as early-life cognitive functioning decreases and early-life physical health declines.

The risk for late-life depressive symptoms is higher among older adults who report a greater number of depressive symptoms in middle age, who have a greater number of stressful life events in early and middle adulthood, and who have lower levels of social support.

the development of predictive models of late-life depressive symptoms, and the identification of the risk factors associated with the onset of depressive symptoms and the maintenance of depressive symptoms over time.
the identification of factors that may be associated with the onset or maintenance of depressive symptoms in late life.
